The count of in-prompt examples separates the first family: zero-shot provides none — instruction only, as in the playlist-title and genre-tagging prompts — single-shot provides one, and few-shot provides several, like the four worked lyric-summary examples. Chain-of-thought is defined by asking the model to reason step by step and show the reasoning, which is the royalty prompt's instruction. A prompt template is about reuse rather than examples: one stored prompt with placeholders filled in per ticket.

questions.question: A public transit agency's rider assistant retrieves community answers from a public suggestion forum. A security review finds that content planted on the forum was ingested into the retrieval corpus, and the assistant now repeats the planted misinformation in its answers. How should this risk be classified?

options.A: Poisoning: the attacker corrupted the retrieval content the assistant depends on, so the planted material now flows into answers through the corpus itself
options.B: Hijacking: the attacker has repurposed the assistant so that it now serves the attacker's task instead of the agency's
options.C: A hosting-layer intrusion: the forum's servers were compromised, so remediation belongs with the forum's hosting provider rather than the AI pipeline
options.D: A content-quality issue: routine moderation review of the forum will surface and remove material of this kind in the normal course

rationale.correct: Adversarial prompt risks are told apart by the attacker's objective: exposure leaks data, poisoning corrupts training or retrieval content, hijacking repurposes the system, and jailbreaking defeats its safety policy. Planting material so that ingestion carries it into the corpus is poisoning precisely because the corruption lives in the content the assistant retrieves — every answer drawing on the tainted corpus spreads it.

distractors.B: Hijacking repurposes the system's behavior toward the attacker's task, typically through crafted input at question time. Here the assistant still performs its own task; what changed is the truthfulness of the content it retrieves.
distractors.C: No server was breached: the attacker used the forum exactly as designed, by posting. The vulnerable boundary is the ingestion of untrusted public content into the corpus, which is squarely a property of the AI pipeline.
distractors.D: Waiting for routine moderation leaves the corpus poisoned for as long as the review cycle runs, with the assistant amplifying the material meanwhile. A risk this direct needs a control at ingestion, not an eventual cleanup.

questions.question: Three teams at an airport ground-operations company edit their shared assistant's production prompt directly in a console. After a quality regression, nobody can say which wording change caused it, when it was made, or how to restore the previous behavior. What practice fixes this class of failure?

options.A: Prompt versioning: manage prompts as versioned artifacts that are tracked, compared, and rolled back like code, with Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management as the AWS home for the practice
options.B: Restricting prompt edits to a single senior engineer, so that changes become rare and the other two teams submit wording requests instead
options.C: A shared log where each team records its prompt changes after making them, so future regressions can be traced by reading the entries
options.D: A weekly regression test of the assistant, so that the next quality drop is noticed within days of the change that caused it

rationale.correct: Prompts that drive production behavior are artifacts, and the failure described — unattributable changes, no history, no rollback — is exactly what versioning exists to remove. Treating prompts as versioned, managed artifacts makes every change tracked, comparable, and reversible, and Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management provides that practice as a service. Three teams can then edit safely because the history, not anyone's memory, carries the record.

distractors.B: Bottlenecking edits through one person reduces the mandate instead of meeting it: three teams legitimately need to iterate, and a single gatekeeper adds queue time while still recording no history and enabling no rollback.
distractors.C: A voluntary after-the-fact log documents changes without governing them: entries get skipped under pressure, the log and the console drift apart, and a written note is still not a diff or a rollback.
distractors.D: Weekly tests shorten the time to notice a regression; they do nothing to attribute it or reverse it. Detection cadence is a complement to version control, not a substitute for it.

questions.question: A dermatology clinic network wants its foundation model to command the field's terminology across every task it performs, and it holds a large unlabeled corpus of de-identified clinical notes. Later, the network plans a smaller, cheaper variant for waiting-room kiosks. Which weight-changing method fits the immediate goal?

options.A: Continuous pre-training on the unlabeled clinical corpus, since the goal is extending domain knowledge across tasks — with distillation reserved for later, when the smaller kiosk model is compressed from the full one
options.B: Fine-tuning on labeled task examples, since tuning on the clinical notes will specialize the model to each dermatology task directly
options.C: Pre-training a new model from scratch on the clinical corpus, so dermatology knowledge is present from the first layer up
options.D: Distillation now, compressing the current model so the network starts from the smaller variant and adds knowledge afterward

rationale.correct: The four ways weights change divide by purpose: pre-training builds general capability, fine-tuning adapts to a task, continuous pre-training extends domain knowledge, and distillation compresses into a smaller model. Broad command of dermatology language across all tasks, fed by a large unlabeled corpus, is continuous pre-training's exact profile — and the kiosk variant is a distillation of the finished model, later.

distractors.B: Fine-tuning adapts a model to a task and expects labeled examples. The corpus is unlabeled and the goal spans every task, which is the domain-extension case, not task adaptation.
distractors.C: From-scratch pre-training rebuilds the general capability the foundation model already has, at the largest possible cost, to reach a goal that extending the existing model achieves for a fraction of it.
distractors.D: Compression is the right method at the wrong point in the sequence: distilling first shrinks a model that does not yet hold the domain knowledge, leaving nothing worth compressing into the kiosks.

questions.question: A life insurance underwriting team ran three tuning efforts: first, teaching a general FM to follow structured directions across many task types using instruction-response pairs; second, specializing a model to actuarial and underwriting language; third, reusing a model trained on health-claims text for a new disability-claims task. Which naming of the three efforts is correct?

options.A: The first is instruction tuning, the second is domain adaptation, and the third is transfer learning — each fine-tuning variant named by its objective
options.B: The first is domain adaptation, the second is instruction tuning, and the third is transfer learning, since teaching direction-following adapts the model to the underwriting domain
options.C: The first is instruction tuning, the second is domain adaptation, and the third is continuous pre-training, since reusing the health-claims model extends its knowledge
options.D: All three are variants of preference alignment, differing only in the data used, so distinguishing them adds vocabulary without a practical difference

rationale.correct: Fine-tuning variants are named by objective. Instruction tuning teaches a model to follow directions, which is the instruction-response effort. Domain adaptation specializes a model to a field's language, which is the actuarial effort. Transfer learning reuses capability learned on one task for a new one, which is the health-claims model applied to disability claims. The names classify the intent of the tuning, not its mechanics.

distractors.B: Swapping the first two names misreads both objectives: direction-following is a general skill across task types, not knowledge of underwriting language, and specializing to a field's vocabulary is not about following directions.
distractors.C: The third effort reuses learned capability on a new task, which is transfer learning; continuous pre-training is the neighboring method that extends domain knowledge with further unlabeled training, and no such training is described.
distractors.D: Collapsing the three names flattens real operational differences — each variant needs different data and serves a different objective, and a team that cannot tell them apart cannot choose or budget between them.

questions.question: A clinical trials recruitment platform is preparing a dataset to fine-tune an FM that screens patient inquiries. The data lead must state what the fine-tuning data has to look like before quality can follow. Which TWO properties belong in that statement? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Labeled examples: each inquiry paired with its correct screening outcome, so the tuning has a signal to learn from
options.B: Representativeness: coverage that mirrors the inquiry traffic the deployed model will actually see in production
options.C: Maximum volume: every inquiry that can be gathered, with quality issues offset by the sheer number of examples
options.D: Strict recency: only inquiries from the last 30 days, since anything older teaches patterns the model should not learn
options.E: Raw authenticity: inquiries left exactly as received, since any curation would introduce the curator's bias into the dataset

rationale.correct: Fine-tuning data earns quality before training starts: it must be curated, governed, sufficiently sized, labeled, and representative of the traffic the model will actually see. Of the options offered, the two that state real requirements are the labeled screening outcomes — without labels there is no tuning signal — and representativeness of production inquiries, without which the model learns a population it will never meet.

distractors.C: Volume does not launder quality: scale multiplies whatever the data contains, including its defects. Sufficient size is a requirement; maximum size with known quality issues is how those issues become model behavior.
distractors.D: A 30-day window is a schedule masquerading as a quality property. Screening patterns do not expire monthly, and truncating history narrows representativeness — the opposite of what the dataset statement needs.
distractors.E: Refusing curation is not neutrality: raw data carries duplicates, errors, and noise, and data curation with governance is itself one of the stated requirements for fine-tuning data. Unprocessed is not unbiased.

questions.question: A fitness app's coaching assistant needs a more motivating tone, but there is no labeled correct answer for what good coaching sounds like. The team does hold thousands of user ratings, each comparing two candidate responses and marking which one the user preferred. Which technique aligns the model using exactly this data?

options.A: Reinforcement learning from human feedback, which aligns model behavior with human preference rankings and exists precisely for goals where no labeled right answer is available to train against
options.B: Supervised fine-tuning on a set of correct coaching responses, so the model learns the target tone from labeled examples
options.C: Raising the temperature so responses vary more, letting warmer phrasings appear more often in the assistant's output
options.D: Publishing tone guidance to users, so they learn to phrase their requests in ways that draw out the coaching style they want

rationale.correct: Reinforcement learning from human feedback aligns model behavior with human preference rankings, and it is used exactly where no labeled right answer exists — quality like motivating tone is comparative, not absolute. The thousands of pairwise preference ratings are RLHF's native input: they teach the model which of two behaviors people prefer, which is the only signal this goal can produce.

distractors.B: Supervised tuning presupposes the labeled correct responses the stem says do not exist. Manufacturing a canonical set of right answers for an inherently preference-shaped quality discards the comparative data the team actually holds.
distractors.C: Temperature widens sampling variety; it has no notion of warmth. More varied output includes more of everything, and no configuration value can convert preference ratings into aligned behavior.
distractors.D: Coaching tone is the product's obligation, not the user's technique. Training users to phrase around a flat assistant assigns the system's gap to its customers while the preference data sits unused.

questions.question: A hotel revenue-management vendor generates pricing-explanation notes with an FM. Quality is subjective — general managers must find a note clear and persuasive — and thousands of notes ship weekly, so evaluation must scale. How should the vendor evaluate?

options.A: Use human-in-the-loop evaluation on a sample to define the subjective standard, then LLM-as-a-judge calibrated against those human judgments to score at weekly scale — the pairing Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation supports
options.B: Score the model on public benchmark datasets, since benchmark results are objective and comparable across model versions
options.C: Rely on account managers hearing from general managers when notes miss the mark, treating complaints as the evaluation channel
options.D: Have the engineer who wrote the note-generation prompt review output samples, since the author knows the intended quality best

rationale.correct: The evaluation approach follows the quality criterion. A subjective bar — clear and persuasive to a general manager — is set by human-in-the-loop evaluation, because only humans hold the standard. Scale then comes from LLM-as-a-judge, calibrated against the human sample so the automated grader applies the human standard weekly, with benchmark datasets reserved for the comparability questions they actually answer, and Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation as the tooling for both.

distractors.B: Public benchmarks measure general capabilities on public tasks; none of them scores whether this vendor's pricing notes persuade this audience. An objective number for the wrong question is not evaluation.
distractors.C: Complaints are the slowest, most filtered signal available: most dissatisfied managers say nothing, and the ones who speak do so weeks into the damage. Waiting for them outsources evaluation to attrition.
distractors.D: The prompt's author reviews from inside the assumptions that shaped the output, which is exactly the anchoring that independent evaluation exists to break. Familiarity with intent is a bias here, not a qualification.

questions.question: A seafood exporter uses an FM to summarize inspection reports, and the team must pick the evaluation metric for the summaries against a set of reference summaries. One engineer proposes BLEU as the industry standard. Which metric choice is right, and what will it not tell the team?

options.A: ROUGE, which measures summarization overlap against the reference summaries — while certifying nothing about factual correctness, which no overlap metric establishes
options.B: BLEU, since it is the established standard for scoring generated text of any kind against references
options.C: BERTScore, since scoring semantic similarity makes overlap counting unnecessary and similar meaning implies the summary is faithful
options.D: No formal metric: have the operations lead spot-read a handful of summaries each Friday and judge quality directly

rationale.correct: Generation metrics map to tasks: ROUGE measures summarization overlap with reference summaries, BLEU measures translation quality, and BERTScore measures semantic similarity. For summaries scored against references, ROUGE is the fitted choice. The second half matters as much: none of the three certifies factual correctness, so a high ROUGE score is overlap evidence, not a guarantee the summary tells the truth about the inspection.

distractors.B: BLEU's home task is translation quality, not summarization: it was designed to compare translated text with reference translations, and applying it across task types misreads what its score means.
distractors.C: BERTScore is the neighboring metric for semantic similarity, and similarity does not imply faithfulness: a summary can sit close to the reference in meaning while misstating the one finding that matters.
distractors.D: Friday spot-reads are opinion sampling: a handful of summaries judged by one reader measures neither coverage nor consistency, and it cannot detect gradual quality drift the way a tracked metric can.

questions.question: A pension fund administrator's RAG assistant answers member questions. The retriever scores well on its retrieval benchmark and the model scores well on its own benchmarks, yet end-to-end answers to real member questions are frequently wrong. What is the evaluation lesson?

options.A: Evaluate the application, not the components: a RAG pipeline is judged end to end on real member questions, because component quality does not compose into system quality
options.B: Re-run each component's benchmark with larger test sets, since the existing scores were probably measured on samples too small to trust
options.C: Re-index the document store more frequently, since strong components with wrong answers usually indicate the retrieval content has gone stale
options.D: Add a notice that answers are informational only, so wrong answers carry less consequence while component scores remain the quality measure

rationale.correct: Applications are evaluated as applications: a RAG pipeline, an agent, or a workflow is judged end to end because component quality does not compose into system quality. A well-benchmarked retriever can fetch passages a well-benchmarked model then misuses — chunk boundaries, prompt assembly, and question mismatch all live between the components. The failing unit is the pipeline, so the evaluation unit must be the pipeline, on real member questions.

distractors.B: Bigger samples of the same component measurements re-answer a question that was never in doubt. Both components already score well; measuring them harder cannot surface a failure that only exists where they meet.
distractors.C: Refresh frequency is one possible cause among many, adopted here without evidence. Tuning a schedule before end-to-end evaluation has localized the failure is intervention by guesswork.
distractors.D: A disclaimer re-labels wrong answers instead of finding out why they happen. Members still receive them, and the measurement gap — no end-to-end evaluation — remains exactly as it was.

questions.question: An industrial equipment rental company has run its GenAI support assistant for two quarters. Model-quality dashboards look strong, and the board now asks whether the assistant actually serves the business. Which TWO metrics answer the board's question? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Task completion rate: the share of customer issues the assistant resolves without a human handoff
options.B: Cost per interaction, compared against the cost of the same interactions handled by the support team
options.C: ROUGE overlap between the assistant's replies and the company's approved answer library
options.D: The assistant's underlying model's ranking on a public GenAI capability leaderboard
options.E: Movement in the company's annual brand-perception survey attributed to the assistant's rollout

rationale.correct: Whether an AI application serves the business is measured by business-alignment metrics: task completion rate, user satisfaction, cost per interaction, conversion rate, and their kin. Task completion rate says whether customers actually get resolved without human handoff, and cost per interaction against the human-handled baseline says what each resolution costs — together they answer value, which no model-quality dashboard can.

distractors.C: Overlap with an answer library is a generation-quality measure on the wrong question: a reply can match the library word for word and still fail to resolve the customer's issue or justify its cost.
distractors.D: A leaderboard ranks the model on public tasks under lab conditions. The board asked about this assistant in this business, and no external ranking carries information about either.
distractors.E: An annual brand survey is a lagging, confounded signal: a year of pricing, fleet, and market changes moves it too, and attribution to the assistant is a guess. Value questions need metrics the assistant directly drives.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical pharmacovigilance team is assembling the training dataset for a model that routes adverse-event reports. The responsible-AI review requires the team to show that the dataset can deliver fairness and inclusivity across patient populations. Which TWO dataset characteristics answer that requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Diverse, curated data sources that span the patient populations, regions, and report types the deployed system will serve
options.B: Balanced datasets, so that no single demographic group or adverse-event class dominates what the model learns
options.C: The largest obtainable volume of reports, since fairness properties emerge on their own once the data is big enough
options.D: Reports drawn exclusively from the company's largest market, since a uniform source keeps the labeling consistent
options.E: A complaint channel opened after deployment, so that reports of biased routing arrive directly from affected users

rationale.correct: The named dimensions of responsible AI — bias, fairness, inclusivity, robustness, safety, veracity — are delivered through dataset characteristics, not declared afterwards: diversity of curated data sources and balanced datasets are the two levers that determine whether every patient population is represented and none dominates. A model routes fairly across groups it has actually seen in fair proportion; both properties are established before training, in the data.

distractors.C: Volume amplifies whatever distribution the data already has: a huge dataset skewed toward one population trains a confidently skewed model. Fairness is a property of composition, and scale is not a substitute for it.
distractors.D: A single-market corpus is uniformity purchased with representativeness: the populations outside that market vanish from the training signal, which is the exact inclusivity failure the review exists to prevent.
distractors.E: A complaint channel discovers unfair routing only after patients have experienced it. Detection after deployment complements responsible data practice; it cannot stand in for building fairness into the dataset.

questions.question: A city parking authority's citizen chatbot must stay on parking topics — no election questions, no legal advice — and must block profanity and personal data in both prompts and responses. One engineer proposes retraining the model until the unwanted behaviors disappear. What is the right control?

options.A: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, enforcing content and topic policy on the model's interactions at the boundary of the prompt and the output, with no retraining of the model at all
options.B: Fine-tuning the unwanted topics and content out of the model, so the policy lives permanently in the weights themselves
options.C: A system-prompt instruction listing the prohibited topics and content, relying on the model to follow the instruction on every interaction
options.D: Replacing free-text chat with a fixed menu of approved canned responses, so off-topic content becomes impossible by construction

rationale.correct: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is the control built for exactly this: enforcing content and topic policy on model interactions — denied topics, filtered content, blocked personal data — applied at the boundary where prompts enter and outputs leave. Constraining behavior at that boundary keeps the policy inspectable and updatable in minutes, rather than baked into weights by retraining.

distractors.B: Tuning behaviors out of a model is slow, expensive, and unverifiable: no training run proves a topic can never resurface, and every policy change becomes another training cycle instead of a configuration edit.
distractors.C: An instruction is a request, not an enforcement point: crafted input can steer a model past its system prompt, which is why policy that must hold belongs in a control layer outside the model rather than in text the model weighs.
distractors.D: Canned menus achieve the policy by deleting the product: citizens lose the free-text help the chatbot exists to provide. The mandate is to make open interaction safe, and guardrails do that without removing the capability.

questions.question: A forestry management SaaS is choosing between a frontier-scale model and a mid-size model that also meets the product's accuracy target. The company's sustainability review flags the energy difference between the two. How should the review's finding be treated?

options.A: As a legitimate selection criterion: larger models cost more energy to train and to run, so with the accuracy target met by both, environmental considerations properly tip the choice to the mid-size model
options.B: As already resolved: modern provider data centers run efficiently, which makes the energy difference between model sizes environmentally immaterial
options.C: As a cost to compensate: choose the frontier-scale model and purchase annual carbon offsets that cover its additional energy footprint
options.D: As premature: revisit environmental questions once the product is profitable, when the company can afford to weigh them properly

rationale.correct: Model choice is an environmental decision: larger models cost more energy to train and to run, and sustainability is a legitimate selection criterion rather than an afterthought. The case here is as clean as it gets — both models meet the accuracy target, so the environmental considerations are not trading against product quality at all; they are simply deciding between two adequate options.

distractors.B: Data-center efficiency scales both models' footprints down proportionally; it does not erase the difference between them. A larger model consumes more energy in the same facility, so the materiality claim is simply not how the physics works.
distractors.C: Offsets compensate for consumption that a better selection would avoid entirely. Paying to neutralize an avoidable footprint treats the ledger while leaving the underlying energy demand — the actual mechanism — untouched.
distractors.D: The energy profile is set at selection time and compounds with every inference from launch onward. Deferring the question until profitability locks in years of the higher footprint that the review exists to prevent.

questions.question: A video game publisher is shipping a GenAI art tool that lets players generate custom character skins. Legal counsel asks what belongs on the risk register specifically because of the generative capability. Which register entry is correct?

options.A: Generated skins may attract intellectual property infringement claims, biased model outputs may harm or exclude players, and both expose the studio to end user risk and the loss of customer trust that follows an incident
options.B: No new entries are needed, since the studio's standard software liability language has always covered whatever its products generate
options.C: The material risks are operational — plan for generation outages and latency spikes, which are what players actually notice and complain about
options.D: Whatever is entered, marketing should keep the generative capability low-profile at launch so that any generated-content incidents draw less public attention

rationale.correct: GenAI creates a distinctive exposure set: intellectual property infringement claims arising from generated output, biased model outputs, end user risk, and the loss of customer trust that follows when either lands in public. A tool that generates player-visible art sits squarely in that set — a skin resembling protected work or an output that demeans a player group is a legal and business event, not a rendering bug.

distractors.B: Boilerplate-covers-everything is a habit applied past its precondition: standard liability language was drafted for software whose outputs the studio authored and reviewed, and generated content is precisely the case it never contemplated.
distractors.C: Outages and latency are real risks of any online feature, offered here in place of the generative ones. Swapping the familiar risk family for the new one leaves the register blind to what the capability actually changes.
distractors.D: Managing attention instead of the risk absorbs a known exposure silently: the incident still happens, players still see it, and the quiet launch reads afterwards as the studio having known and said nothing.

questions.question: A warehouse robotics integrator's visual defect-detection model scores 99% on its training images but 71% on validation images and live camera feeds. Analysis also shows the misses concentrate on one product line's packaging. What is the correct reading of the scores?

options.A: The model is overfitting — strong training performance with weak validation and production performance means it memorized training specifics rather than learning the general pattern, and the concentrated misses show a fit failure falling unevenly on one group of products
options.B: The model is underfitting — it is too simple to capture the task, which is why the two scores diverge, and more capacity will close the gap
options.C: The validation set is unrepresentatively hard — re-draw the validation split until the two scores align, then reassess whether any problem remains
options.D: The gap is camera noise — live lenses and lighting degrade inputs relative to the training images, and the scores will converge as the hardware is maintained

rationale.correct: The score pattern is the diagnostic: strong training but weak validation or production performance means overfitting — the model bound itself to training-image specifics that do not generalize — while weak performance on both would mean underfitting. The 99% against 71% split reads cleanly as the former, and the misses concentrating on one product line show why fit matters beyond averages: either failure can fall unevenly across groups.

distractors.B: Underfitting shows as weak performance on training and validation alike, because the model never captured the pattern at all. A 99% training score is the opposite signature: this model captured too much, too specifically.
distractors.C: Re-drawing the split until the numbers agree is measuring for the answer you want: the divergence is the finding, and the live camera feeds — which no split touches — already confirm it is real.
distractors.D: The stem says validation images show the same 71%, and validation sets are not affected by lens wear. A hardware explanation that cannot account for the validation gap is attributing the failure to the wrong mechanism.

questions.question: A mortgage origination firm's pre-qualification model reports 90% aggregate accuracy. A community advocacy group alleges the model performs worse for applicants from certain neighborhoods, and the firm must actually find out. How is bias like this discovered in practice?

options.A: Subgroup analysis comparing per-group accuracy across neighborhoods and demographics, analysis of label quality in the historical decisions, and human audits — with Amazon A2I bringing structured human review into the loop
options.B: Recomputing aggregate accuracy on a fresh sample of applications, since a sound overall number on new data would settle the allegation
options.C: Enabling drift monitoring on the production model, since a bias problem of this kind would register as distribution drift in the monitoring dashboards
options.D: Publishing the model's aggregate accuracy and methodology in a transparency report, so external parties can see the firm has nothing to hide

rationale.correct: Bias hides inside aggregates, so it is found by disaggregating: subgroup analysis compares accuracy per group, where a model that is 90% accurate overall can be sharply worse for one neighborhood; analysis of label quality asks whether the historical decisions the model learned from were themselves skewed; and human audits examine individual decisions — the loop Amazon A2I exists to structure.

distractors.B: A fresh sample re-measures the same aggregate, and the aggregate is the number that conceals the problem. The allegation is about a subgroup, and no overall score, however fresh, speaks to it.
distractors.C: Drift monitoring detects the input population changing over time — an adjacent job. A model that has been uneven across neighborhoods since launch shows no drift while the unfairness continues undetected.
distractors.D: A transparency report discloses the number that hides the issue. Publishing methodology has governance value, but disclosure is not discovery: it cannot tell the firm whether the allegation is true.

questions.question: A banking regulator sends a community bank two requests about its loan-decision model: documentation of what the system is and how it was built, and an account of why one named applicant was declined. The project lead plans a single response document. What should the lead understand first?

options.A: These are different properties: transparency exposes what the system is and how it was built, while explainability accounts for why a particular output happened — the regulator asked for both, and each needs its own kind of artifact
options.B: Publishing the architecture and training-data description satisfies both requests, since a system that is fully documented is by that fact explainable
options.C: Neither request can be met for a model of this complexity, so the bank should seek a supervisory exemption rather than attempt either response
options.D: A notice that lending decisions involve an AI system, added to all decline letters, addresses the regulator's underlying concern in both requests

rationale.correct: Transparent and explainable are different properties answering different questions. Transparency is systemic: what the model is, what data built it, how it was assembled — the first request. Explainability is per-output: why this applicant received this decision — the second request. Because the properties differ, so do the artifacts: system documentation cannot account for one declined application, and one decision's account documents nothing about the system.

distractors.B: Documentation makes a system transparent; it does not make any individual decision explainable. The regulator's second request names one applicant, and no architecture description answers why that person was declined.
distractors.C: Declining both requests abandons obligations the bank can meet: transparency artifacts exist for any model, and explainability techniques and interpretable-model choices exist precisely for regulated decisions like lending.
distractors.D: A notice that AI is involved discloses the system's existence — the thinnest slice of transparency — and explains nothing. Neither request is answered by labeling the decision as automated.

questions.question: A life insurance underwriter must show its board how explainability will actually reach the people who need it — reviewers, auditors, and applicants — for its new risk-assessment model. Which set of artifacts and mechanisms does that job?

options.A: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards documenting the model's purpose and limitations, SageMaker Clarify surfacing bias findings and feature attributions, disclosure of open source components and licensing, and human-centered design with user-feedback mechanisms
options.B: AWS KMS encryption of the model artifacts and CloudTrail logging of every API call, establishing a complete audited record around the model
options.C: A public trust page describing the company's commitment to responsible AI, professionally written to reassure applicants and regulators
options.D: Deferral until the model can be replaced by a fully open source alternative, since meaningful explainability artifacts are not possible before then

rationale.correct: Explainability travels to people through named carriers: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards state a model's purpose, limitations, and intended use in reviewable form; SageMaker Clarify surfaces bias findings and feature attributions that account for outputs; open source and licensing disclosure shows what the system is built from; and human-centered design with user-feedback mechanisms gives the people affected a channel back. Together they are how explainability becomes something reviewers and applicants can actually hold.

distractors.B: Encryption and API logging are security and audit controls — the adjacent governance job. A perfectly encrypted, fully logged model can remain entirely unexplained to every reviewer and applicant who encounters it.
distractors.C: A trust page is reassurance, not explainability: it carries no model card, no attribution, no limitation statement — nothing a reviewer could use to understand a single decision.
distractors.D: Model Cards, Clarify findings, and feedback mechanisms work on the current model today. Waiting for a future open source replacement withholds available artifacts for the entire life of the deployed system.

questions.question: A hospital radiology group is selecting a triage model that prioritizes scans for radiologist review. A deep ensemble scores 94% but its reasoning is opaque; an interpretable model scores 91% and clinicians can read the factors behind each priority score. The medical board must be able to defend every triage decision. Which choice is right?

options.A: The 91% interpretable model: the models that perform best are often the hardest to interpret, and a regulated, high-stakes decision can force the more interpretable, lower-performing choice — this is that case
options.B: The 94% ensemble: accuracy improvements translate directly into patient safety, so the stronger model is the responsible pick whatever its opacity
options.C: The 94% ensemble, paired with a second model that generates a plausible explanation for each triage output after the fact
options.D: Whichever model the deployment team prefers: model selection is an engineering detail that does not need to reach the medical board at all

rationale.correct: The safety-transparency trade-off is real: interpretability and performance often pull against each other, and the models that score highest are frequently the hardest to account for. When the decision is high-stakes and must be defensible — a medical board standing behind every triage call — the trade-off resolves toward the interpretable model, accepting 91% over 94% because a decision nobody can explain is not defensible at any accuracy.

distractors.B: Higher-accuracy-is-always-safer is a slogan that ignores this scenario's binding constraint: the board must defend individual decisions, and an opaque model leaves it defending outputs it cannot account for — including the errors the stronger model still makes.
distractors.C: A second model rationalizing outputs after the fact produces plausible stories, not the actual factors behind the score. Post-hoc narrative is interpretability's look-alike, and a medical board defending decisions with it is defending fiction.
distractors.D: Routing the choice away from the board hides a trade-off that belongs to the accountable owner: the board carries the defense obligation, so the interpretability consequence of the model choice is exactly what it must see.
